column4: This ayah announces the believers' success; the next ayah specifies humility in prayer, making success and attentive salat a direct pairing like 87:14-15.
This ayah's own contribution is humility within prayer; 23:1 frames that manner of salat as a mark of the successful believers.
The passage closes its description of believers by saying they guard their prayers, a specific form of sustained salat alongside the section's closing prayer act.
The ayah joins fear of God unseen, establishing prayer, and purification; it gathers the section's fear, salat, and tazkiya strands in one statement.
The command to establish prayer at the day's edges is followed by the claim that good deeds remove wrong and that this is a reminder for those who remember, directly joining salat and dhikr.

In fear, prayer may be performed on foot or riding; when safe, believers are told to remember Allah. This ayah's own contribution is the bodily adaptation of salat and its transition to remembrance in safety.
This ayah permits shortening prayer during travel when believers fear attack; 4:102 supplies the following bodily arrangement for prayer in danger.
The successors are said to have let prayer go to waste and followed desires, the direct contrary of remembering the Lord and praying in 87:15.
Those who forget Allah are made to forget themselves; this gives the section's remembrance and forgetting motif a direct reversal and consequence.
In the scene of meeting an enemy force, believers are told to remember Allah much so that they may prosper, joining abundant dhikr to success as 87:14-15 do.
The list of faithful men and women includes those who remember Allah much and promises forgiveness and reward, a repeated formulation of abundant dhikr.
This ayah opens the instruction to stand in prayer through the night; 73:4 specifies measured Quran recitation within the same night practice.
This ayah sets the night prayer's duration at half the night or a little less; it gives the bodily practice in 73:2 a concrete measure.
The Prophet is told to recite the Quran with measured recitation within the night vigil, explicitly combining prayer and Quran reading.
The command to magnify the Lord is a parallel devotional formulation to 87:1's glorification of the Lord's name, though it uses كبر rather than the section's root س ب ح.
Believers are told to call on their Lord humbly and privately; it meets the section's dictionary sense of salat as supplication and its public/private speech detail.
The call to invoke God in fear and hope gives supplication the same fear stance that the section links to remembering the reminder.
Zakariya calls on his Lord with a private call, a specific scene of supplication and hidden speech that joins the section's dua and public/private details.
This ayah names Moses and Aaron's revelation as light and a reminder for the God-fearing, connecting the section's reference to Moses with Quranic remembrance.
This ayah's own contribution is identifying the righteous as those who fear their Lord unseen and dread the Hour; 21:48 supplies their reminder from Moses and Aaron.
After completing the rites, people are told to remember Allah with abundant remembrance; it makes remembrance the continuation of bodily worship, as 87:15 joins remembrance and prayer.
Every community is given a rite so that its people may mention Allah's name over the provision of livestock; this links remembrance of the Lord's name to embodied worship and provision.
The ayah says neither the animals' flesh nor blood reaches God, but piety does; it clarifies that an outward ritual act is not itself the inward worship emphasized by the section.
The faithful are described as praising God, bowing, and prostrating; this directly joins praise to the bodily acts that the section includes in salat.
The maintainers of God's mosques establish prayer, give zakat, and fear God alone; it is a positive counterpart to 24:36-37's worship-house and undistracted men.

Abraham and Ishmael are commanded to purify the House for those who circle it, stay there, bow, and prostrate; this links sacred place, purification, and the bodily acts in the section's prayer definition.
This continuation asks whether the servant being forbidden is on guidance; 96:10 identifies the interrupted act as prayer, so this ayah specifies the worshipper's stance.
This ayah asks whether the praying servant enjoins mindfulness of God, continuing the contrast between the one who prays and the one who obstructs him.
This continuation asks whether the one forbidding prayer denies and turns away; its own contribution is the opponent's refusal, completing the scene that begins in 96:9-10.
The ayah asks whether the opponent knows that Allah sees him; it completes the prayer-obstruction scene and echoes the section's claim that God knows what is public and hidden.
